Jersey City by the numbers

Which Jersey City offices handle property tax?

Jersey City splits the work between a Tax Assessor, who sets and records values, and a Tax Collector, who sends the bills and takes payment. The collector's counter is at 280 Grove Street, Room 101, and serves the public each business day between 8:30 and 4:30. Mail goes to the City of Jersey City Tax Collector at that address, with checks or money orders made out to the same name. The city's property tax page also lists online payment and a bank-debit option that uses a signed authorization form.

The assessor's page tells owners how to look up an assessment: open the state-hosted tax records site, choose Hudson County and Jersey City, then search by street address, owner name or block and lot. The same page links the forms most sellers and heirs end up needing, including veteran deduction claims, exemption claims and the five-year exemption and abatement application.

One note on the city's separate tax page: it describes a payroll tax on employers, and resident wages are exempt. That levy is unrelated to your home.

What are the Jersey City property tax due dates?

The city's property tax page names the first of February, May, August and November. Those dates track the state schedule in N.J.S.A. 54:4-66. Before you count on paying a few days late, ask the collector how much grace the city allows.

Jersey City installments and how each amount is set
InstallmentDue dateHow the amount is figured
FirstFebruary 1One quarter of the prior year's tax
SecondMay 1One quarter of the prior year's tax
ThirdAugust 1Half of the current levy left after the first two payments
FourthNovember 1The other half of that remaining current levy

Source: City of Jersey City property tax page; N.J.S.A. 54:4-66(a) and (c).

A missed quarter stays delinquent, with interest, until every tax and lien due on the property is cleared. Paying ahead is allowed, and interest only starts after the delinquency date.

How high is the tax rate in Jersey City?

The Division of Taxation's 2025 table gives Jersey City a general rate of 2.335 and an effective rate of 1.847. The effective rate restates that levy against estimated full value, which makes it the fairer yardstick when you compare towns. Among the county's twelve municipalities Jersey City falls in the middle on the effective measure, higher than Hoboken at 1.070 and lower than Bayonne at 1.987.

The city's last full revaluation of every property took place in 2017, carried out in response to a state order. Assessments since then are updated by the assessor's office. Before listing, pull the latest assessment for your block and lot and set it beside recent nearby sale prices.

Source: NJ Division of Taxation, 2025 General Tax Rates; Jersey City revaluation page.

Can I appeal a Jersey City assessment?

Yes, through the Hudson County Board of Taxation rather than any city office. The assessor's page links the county petition and its instructions, and the county accepts filings online, in person on Cornelison Avenue, or by mail after a call to (201) 395-6260. Revaluation shifted every Jersey City assessment in 2017, which makes the facts behind an old appeal worth rechecking today. Keep these points in mind:

  • Cutoff: April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation or reassessment, with extra time when notices are mailed late.
  • Proof: sales from before the October 1 assessment date, with photographs, carry the argument.
  • Attendance: skipping the hearing can produce a dismissal that also closes the door to Tax Court.
  • Payoff: a reduction holds for the appeal year and the two after it.

Source: NJ Division of Taxation guide to tax appeal hearings; Hudson County Division of Tax Assessments.

What is the Jersey City housing market like by the numbers?

Jersey City spreads 292,449 residents (2020 census) across 14.74 square miles of land, or about 19,835 per square mile, and the 2025 estimate stands at 302,013. Owners live in just 27.9 percent of the homes. For 2020 to 2024 the middle owned home was worth $566,900, rent in the middle ran $2,007 and a typical household brought in $97,710.

The city has 125,223 households averaging 2.33 people. Foreign-born residents make up 41.7 percent of the population, and 50.9 percent of residents age five and older speak a language other than English at home. A seller here is usually dealing with a market where most neighbors rent, so a house with tenants is a common situation.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts.

How does the shape of Jersey City affect a house sale?

Only Newark has more people than Jersey City among New Jersey cities, and Jersey City is the Hudson County seat. Water frames it: the Hudson River and Upper New York Bay to the east, the Hackensack River and Newark Bay to the west. It has about 30.7 miles of waterfront and a long history as a port and rail terminus. The present city took shape in 1870 when Jersey City, Hudson City and Bergen merged, and Greenville was added three years later.

Those layers produce distinct areas that buyers search by name: Paulus Hook and the downtown waterfront, Journal Square, Bergen Hill, the Heights and Greenville in the south. The waterfront has a flood record, since Hurricane Irene's storm surge flooded parts of downtown in August 2011. Check flood exposure on a waterfront or low block before you price the house or discuss repairs. The city connects to Manhattan through the Holland Tunnel, PATH, NJ Transit buses and NY Waterway ferries.

Source: Jersey City, New Jersey (Wikipedia).

What local features come up in Jersey City listings?

Water and open space show up often in how Jersey City homes are described. The Hudson River Waterfront Walkway, required of waterfront developers by state rule since 1988, runs from Hoboken Terminal through Liberty State Park to Port Liberte. Inland, Reservoir No. 3 is now a passive recreation area, and Pershing Field occupies the site planned for a Reservoir No. 2 that was never built. Port Jersey handles container shipping on the Newark Bay side.

Journal Square takes its name from the newspaper that moved there in 1911, and Hudson County Community College opened in the same district in 1974. Buyers who ask about such landmarks are usually asking about commutes and street noise, so expect questions about distance to PATH, buses and ferries when you list.

Source: Jersey City, New Jersey (Wikipedia).

How should a seller handle tax owed on a Jersey City house?

Start with the assessment search so you know the block and lot on record, then ask the collector for the balance by quarter. Three items cause most surprises: a quarter that went delinquent, a tax lien held by a third party, and a bill for an abatement payment, which the city's payment page routes to its own portal. If the house has a five-year exemption or abatement, confirm that its payment is current before closing.

  • Bring the block and lot, the owner's name and the property address when you call the collector.
  • Ask for a written payoff figure good through the closing date.
  • Ask the assessor whether a veteran or senior deduction on the property ends with the sale.
  • Inherited houses may carry unpaid quarters from before the owner's death, so check them first.

More questions about Jersey City, NJ Property Tax Guide

What are the due dates for property tax in Jersey City?

Four dates a year: the first of February, May, August and November. The collector can confirm any grace period.

Where can I pay a Jersey City property tax bill in person?

The Tax Collector's office is at 280 Grove Street, Room 101, and serves walk-in payers each business day between 8:30 and 4:30. Online and mailed payments are accepted too.

How do I look up my Jersey City assessment?

Open the tax records site linked on the assessor's page, select Hudson County and Jersey City, then search by address, owner or block and lot.

When did Jersey City last revalue every property?

In 2017, following a state order. The assessor's office has maintained values since.

Does a Jersey City appeal go to the city or the county?

The county board hears it, and the city does not. Its usual cutoff is April 1, with May 1 applying after a revaluation.

Newark by the numbers

Which Newark office sends the property tax bill?

The City of Newark Department of Finance bills and collects it, and Essex County is the county that hears assessment appeals. Inside Finance, the Assessments unit decides what real estate is taxable, keeps a tax map for every parcel and records ownership and mortgage changes. Revenue Collections sends the bills, takes the payments and runs enforcement when taxes go unpaid.

To learn what a Newark property owes, call customer service Monday through Friday, 9 am to 4 pm, except holidays. The tax lines are 973-733-3791, 973-733-3792, 973-733-3962, 973-733-8098 and 973-733-3978. The city's Payment Center also takes online tax payments by credit card, debit card or electronic check.

When are Newark property taxes due?

Installments are due on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, the quarterly dates that apply across New Jersey. Late amounts can carry interest of up to 8 percent on the first $1,500 and up to 18 percent above that, plus a penalty of up to 6 percent for delinquencies above $10,000 when the fiscal year closes.

Newark applies a partial payment to the oldest quarter outstanding. A homeowner who owes the first three quarters and sends money in September sees it go against the first quarter's principal and interest, so the later quarters stay open. That matters for a seller, because the payoff on the closing statement can be larger than a quick tally of the latest bill suggests.

What happens to a Newark house when taxes go unpaid?

The city sells a tax lien certificate on it. Newark runs a standard tax sale for prior years' taxes and charges that are still owing, and an accelerated tax sale for the current year's charges that remain due after the statutory date of November 10. Its Finance page cites N.J.S.A. 54:5-19 for taxes outstanding from the prior year.

  • The buyer of the certificate holds a lien and does not take title at the auction.
  • A town holder can sue to foreclose six months after the sale, and a private holder can sue after two years.
  • An owner can demand in writing, before final judgment, that the property go to a sheriff's sale so any equity is protected.
  • Redemption stays open until the Superior Court enters a judgment barring it.

Our New Jersey tax sale guide covers redemption costs and the equity demand in detail.

Where do I file an appeal of a Newark assessment?

File with the Essex County Board of Taxation on Form A-1, together with the comparable sales form that goes with it. The petition must be filed and received by April 1, or by May 1 when a municipal revaluation or reassessment has been done. For a property assessed above $1,000,000, the owner may file directly with the State Tax Court instead.

The burden sits with the owner. You have to show that the assessed value is unreasonable compared with a market value standard. An assessment counts as excessive or discriminatory only if it fails both the true market value standard and the common level range, which is plus or minus 15 percent of the district's average ratio.

  • A judgment from the county board can be appealed to the Tax Court of New Jersey within 45 days.
  • An added or omitted assessment, which arises when changes are made to a property after October 1, is appealed on Form AA-1.
  • An added assessment above $750,000 in total may go directly to the Tax Court.

What does Newark look like for a house seller?

Puritans from the New Haven Colony settled Newark in 1666, and it became a city on April 11, 1836. It is the county seat of Essex County and New Jersey's largest city, with a Census Bureau estimate of 323,808 residents for July 2025 on 24.14 square miles of land. Most households rent, so a seller often deals with tenants already in the building. The city has five wards, and heavily industrial land around the airport and seaport sits mostly in the East and South wards, while homes cluster in the North, Central and West wards.

Newark housing and income facts, Census Bureau QuickFacts

The land slopes from about 230 feet in the western section down to sea level in the east, in a basin that drains toward the Passaic River. Historically the higher ground, around Forest Hill, High Street and Weequahic, drew the wealthier families. The East Ward's Ironbound is a dense district of apartment buildings and rowhouses, while the marshes on Newark Bay were reclaimed in the 1920s for the airport and Port Newark.

Which Newark neighborhoods and roads shape a sale?

Each ward has its own housing mix. The North Ward is centered on Branch Brook Park and takes in Broadway, Mount Pleasant, Upper Roseville and Forest Hill, where the Forest Hill Historic District holds older mansions and colonial homes. The West Ward covers Vailsburg, Ivy Hill, the West Side, Fairmount and Lower Roseville. The South Ward includes Weequahic, Clinton Hill and Dayton, and the Central Ward holds University Heights and Government Center.

Newark is served by the New Jersey Turnpike (Interstate 95), Interstate 280, Interstate 78, the Garden State Parkway, U.S. Routes 1/9 and 22, and Route 21. Newark Penn Station, east of downtown, carries PATH, NJ Transit and Amtrak trains, and the Newark Light Rail links it to Broad Street Station. In 2020, 40.3 percent of Newark households had no car, so a short walk to transit is a real selling point for many buyers.

More than 100,000 people commute to Newark each workday, and nearly 50,000 students attend its universities and medical and law schools. Newark Public Schools is the largest school system in the state.

How should I handle tax due when I sell a Newark house?

Ask Revenue Collections for a written statement covering every unpaid quarter, interest and any tax sale certificate, dated to the closing day. Whoever handles the closing pays that balance from the seller's proceeds, which clears the lien for the buyer.

  • List every quarter that is open, including prior-year balances, since those can already be in a tax sale.
  • Check whether a certificate was sold and recorded, and who holds it.
  • If an assessment appeal is pending, tell your closing attorney so the filing is accounted for at closing.
  • Plan for the seller-paid realty transfer fee on the deed.

More questions about Newark, NJ Property Tax Guide

Who do I call to find out what I owe on a Newark house?

Call Newark's Finance customer service on a weekday between 9 am and 4 pm at 973-733-3791, one of five tax lines the city lists. Ask for the amount through your closing date.

By what date must a Newark assessment petition arrive?

The deadline is April 1, or May 1 if a revaluation or reassessment was done. File Form A-1 with the Essex County Board of Taxation. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 can go straight to the Tax Court.

What interest does Newark charge on late taxes?

Interest can reach 8 percent on the first $1,500 and 18 percent on the balance above that, under state law. A penalty of up to 6 percent can follow when the delinquency is over $10,000 at year end.

Does paying part of my bill stop a tax sale?

A partial payment is credited to the oldest quarter first, which cuts that quarter's principal and interest but leaves later quarters open. Newark can still sell a certificate for prior years' taxes that remain unpaid.

Can I sell a Newark house that has a tax sale certificate on it?

Yes. The certificate amount and its interest come out of the sale price at closing, and the holder then discharges the lien. Get the payoff from the tax collector in writing so the title company can wire the exact amount.

Which Edison offices send and collect the tax bill?

Over 30,000 tax accounts, and about as many sewer accounts, run through Edison's Tax Collector. Walk-in service is on the second floor at the municipal building, 100 Municipal Blvd., on weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4:30 in the afternoon, and the office answers 732-248-7228 and TaxCollector@EdisonNJ.gov. The Tax Assessor, a separate office, keeps data on more than 28,000 properties and takes the state deduction applications.

Because Edison lies in Middlesex County, a formal challenge to value is heard by that county's tax board, and the assessor works with it on the township tax map. The collector cannot change a value, and the assessor cannot take a payment, so the first call depends on whether your question is about the amount of value or the amount due.

  • Collector: bills, receipts, payoff figures and sewer accounts.
  • Assessor: ownership records, property data, mailing address changes and deductions.
  • County board: formal appeals of value.

What is Edison like as a housing market?

Edison is a 30-square-mile township of roughly 109,000 people in the Raritan Valley, and it wraps around the borough of Metuchen. Thomas Edison's Menlo Park laboratory, where the light bulb was perfected, gave the township its name in 1954, replacing the old name of Raritan Township. About 27 miles separate it from both Midtown Manhattan and Trenton.

The economy rests on Raritan Center, a 2,300-acre business park that includes the New Jersey Convention and Exposition Center, with regional distribution hubs for national carriers. Older manufacturing left the area in the 2000s, and the Ford plant that once stood in Edison was demolished by 2008 and replaced with retail. Neighborhood names on a listing include Menlo Park, Oak Tree, Clara Barton, Stelton, Raritan Manor and Lincoln Park. Route 1, Route 27, Route 440 and Interstate 287 cross Edison, and the New Jersey Turnpike has its Exit 10 here. Two high schools, Edison High in the south and J.P. Stevens in the north, split the public school district of 19 schools.

The township counts about 307 miles of roadway, and it maintains 257 of them, with Middlesex County, the state and the Turnpike Authority covering the rest. Edison winters are cool to cold with snow every year, and summers run hot and humid, so roof, gutter and drainage condition tend to come up in inspections.

  • Census estimate for July 2025: 109,077 people, against 107,400 at the 2020 base.
  • Typical home value for 2020 through 2024: $496,900.
  • Owners live in 60.6 percent of homes, and median gross rent is $1,974.
  • Median household income: $125,145, with 47.7 percent of residents foreign-born.

When is Edison property tax due?

Edison's four installments land on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, each followed by ten days of grace that stretch to Monday when the tenth falls on a weekend. Bills go out once a year, usually in June or July, with four stubs: August and November of the current year and February and May of the next. If no bill has arrived by August 1, call the collector, because a missing bill still leaves you responsible.

Edison installment schedule, per the Tax Collector's billing notice
InstallmentDue date
Third quarterAugust 1
Fourth quarterNovember 1
First quarterFebruary 1
Second quarterMay 1

A late payment accrues interest of up to 8 percent annually on $1,500 and 18 percent on the remainder, measured from the original due date after grace ends. Total delinquency past $10,000 at year end can add a surcharge of up to 6 percent. Any municipal charge still unpaid on November 11 is subject to the tax sale.

How do you pay in Edison, and what happens with a mortgage escrow?

Options include cash, check or money order at the counter upstairs, the curbside drop box, a mailed check, or the online payment page linked from the township site. A mailed check counts when it lands in the office, whatever the postmark says, and drop box deposits post the following business day. Write checks to Edison Tax Collector, leave off any future date, and plan for a $20 fee if one bounces.

  • With an escrow account, the lender gets the original bill and you get an advice copy.
  • Paid off your mortgage? You can use the advice copy to make the next payment and tell the collector who now pays.
  • Want a mailed receipt? Return the whole bill with a prepaid return envelope.

How is an Edison sewer bill different from the tax bill?

One sewer bill goes out each year, drawn from the previous year's water consumption, and it can be paid in two halves. Stub one carries its own due date, usually in the April to June stretch, and stub two falls due October 1. The owner is responsible, and sewer sits outside the monthly mortgage payment.

Residential customers get a 15 percent outside water discount that is already taken off the bill. A rate freeze on a primary residence goes to owners 65 and up who show proof of age by March 1, and signing up for a Senior Center card counts as proof. At a sale, the sewer bill passes to the buyer or title company, which makes it worth confirming that both accounts are current.

Can you contest an Edison assessment?

A petition goes to the Middlesex County Board of Taxation. It is due April 1, shifting to May 1 after a township revaluation, and it must arrive by then. Copies go to the Edison assessor and clerk. The case turns on value alone, argued with as many as five comparable sales priced as of the previous October 1.

Fees scale with assessed value from $5 to $150, and a board judgment stays in force for three tax years unless something alters the assessment. Call the Middlesex board for its hearing schedule, and the Edison assessor for questions on the property record card. The assessor's office also processes the $250 deductions for qualified veterans, seniors and disabled owners, plus the full exemption for a 100 percent disabled veteran.

What if Edison tax is owed when the house sells?

A house can sell with tax unpaid. The closing agent settles the amount out of the sale money, working from a payoff the collector dates for closing day. Ask for the per-day interest too, because a short delay moves the number.

The state homeowner guide explains that a balance left after the November installment can become a lien, that the lien has to be redeemed before a sale, and that a lien holder may start foreclosure once two years pass. In Edison, a balance left on November 11 is eligible for the tax sale. Settling it before listing keeps the sale simpler, and the Tax Collector can also tell you whether the sewer account carries a balance of its own. Sewer charges unpaid on November 11 face the same tax sale exposure as property tax. For a quick look at an account, the township's tax record search shows the current status.

More questions about Edison, NJ Property Tax Guide

What is the Edison Tax Collector's address?

On the second floor of the municipal building at 100 Municipal Blvd., Edison, NJ 08817, open weekdays until 4:30 p.m. The phone is 732-248-7228.

How long is the Edison tax grace period?

Ten days, counted from the due date on the stub, with a weekend ending pushed to Monday.

When is the second Edison sewer payment due?

October 1. Stub one shows the due date for the first half, usually in spring.

Does a postmark count for an Edison payment?

No. The office must receive the payment by the end of the grace period, and drop box payments are posted the next business day.

Which county board hears Edison appeals?

The Middlesex County Board of Taxation, by April 1, or May 1 after a township-wide revaluation.

When are Hoboken property taxes due?

Hoboken follows the quarterly calendar that N.J.S.A. 54:4-66 sets for towns on a calendar fiscal year: the first day of February, May, August and November. One bill arrives each year, carrying four payment stubs. Early payments are allowed, and the earlier ones are estimates because the true levy is not yet known.

The collector's page prints the grace-period end date for each quarter only as a graphic, so read the date on your stub or call ext. 1220 before you mail anything. The office does not honor postmarks. A payment has to reach the office, the box or the online portal by the last day of grace. Anything later carries interest running from the original due date.

A payment drop box sits just inside the Newark Street entrance of City Hall. The office itself shuts on city holidays and weekends.

What is the property tax rate in Hoboken?

The state's 2025 table lists Hoboken at a general rate of 1.805 and an effective rate of 1.070, the lowest effective rate of the twelve Hudson County municipalities in that table. The general rate is charged on every hundred dollars of assessed value. As a rough illustration, a home assessed at $600,000 would owe about $10,830 a year at 1.805. The effective rate restates the burden against estimated true value, which lets owners compare towns whose assessments sit at different levels.

The city introduced a $152 million municipal budget for 2026 and described a projected municipal tax impact of under 19 percent, or roughly $130 more per quarter for the average assessed property compared with 2025. Your own bill shows what was finally adopted, so use it rather than a news figure when you plan a sale.

Source: NJ Division of Taxation 2025 General Tax Rates; City of Hoboken budget announcement.

What is the process for contesting a Hoboken assessment?

Appeals go to the Hudson County Board of Taxation, and the Hoboken assessor's page carries the appeal forms. The state sets April 1 as the usual cutoff, so the 2026 window is behind us. The next one closes April 1 of the following year, or May 1 if the city completes a revaluation. A petition should include three to five comparable sales that predate the October 1 assessment date, plus photos.

The collector's page spells out how a county judgment reaches your account:

  • Nothing can be calculated until the county certifies the tax rate.
  • The credit lands on fourth-quarter tax first, then on any unpaid third-quarter balance.
  • If credit remains, it is refunded to the petitioner or to the lawyer who filed for them.
  • The next year's first two quarters reflect the lower figure, and a revised bill goes to the owner and the mortgage company on record.

Which other Hoboken tax bills fall outside the quarterly cycle?

A few charges do not follow the four-stub pattern, and each one can surface during a sale.

  • Lien redemptions. Ask the collector for a redemption statement before you pay. Balances shown on the city website may be off, and payment must be by certified check or money order.

The state's $250 senior and disabled deduction asks for a year of New Jersey residence, ownership and occupancy of the home on October 1, and income under the limit. Once granted it must be renewed with Form PD5, filed with the collector by March 1.

What do Census figures say about housing in Hoboken?

The 2020 count put 60,419 people onto Hoboken's 1.25 square miles, about 48,335 for each one, and the newest federal estimate is 59,027. The city's 28,088 households average 2.02 people, and degree holders make up 82.6 percent of adults. Commutes average 36.8 minutes. Small households, a renter majority and high values shape the market, and the street grid of named avenues crossing numbered streets holds most of the sales.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts.

How does an unpaid tax bill affect selling a house in Hoboken?

A quarter left unpaid after its grace period becomes delinquent and keeps accruing interest until all taxes and liens are paid, so a seller with a past-due balance has to clear it or have the closing pay it. Request a written payoff or redemption figure from the collector close to the closing date, since interest changes the number. Ask whether any added assessment bill is still on the way if you renovated.

Taxes paid ahead of a due date are accepted at any time under the statute, and no interest builds before the delinquency date. A condominium owner should also confirm whether the Special Improvement District charge sits on the bill. Even an as-is purchase ends with a deed recorded at the county, so settle the tax status before that step.

Are Hoboken property taxes paid quarterly?

The reverse holds on the state's measure: 1.070 effective is the lowest of the twelve towns. High home values still produce sizable bills.

Expect a credit rather than an instant check. It goes against the later quarters first and any excess is refunded, but only after the county certifies the rate.

Value is a separate matter. The township assessor sets assessments, and appeals go to the Camden County Board of Taxation in Blackwood, and the collector has no role in them. The township spreads over 24.07 square miles in northern Camden County, with Pennsauken Creek as its eastern edge and the Cooper River along its southern line. It began as Delaware Township in 1844, took the Cherry Hill name in 1961, and grew in the postwar suburban boom around the Cherry Hill Mall, which opened in October 1961 as the first enclosed mall in the eastern United States. Before that, Quaker settlers founded a hamlet called Colestown in the late 1600s, and 19th century farms in the township supplied produce to the Campbell's plant in Camden. The township's quarterly dates are August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. A ten-day cushion follows each one, and a tenth day that falls on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday carries the cushion to the next working day. The office mails bills twice a year: in July for the third and fourth quarters and in January for the first and second. A bill that never shows up does not cancel the payment or the interest.

Money has to reach the office before the grace period ends, because New Jersey does not allow the collector to accept postmarks. Once the cushion ends, interest is charged retroactively: 8 percent annually on the first slice of $1,500 behind, 18 percent annually on the remainder. The counter and the staff phone line do not take cards. The office also sends email reminders about a week before each due date to residents who sign up.

What does Cherry Hill charge for sewer, and who gets a discount?

A flat annual fee covers residential sewer and falls due April 1. Commercial sewer follows water use and is billed in two parts, due the first of November and the first of May. A 10 percent reduction is available to owners aged 60 and up who live in the house and show the Tax Collector proof of age. Sewer is billed apart from tax, so the closing agent should ask the collector whether it is paid to date.

Is a Cherry Hill assessment open to challenge?

Yes. Camden County's tax board hears the case, with filing closing April 1 or, right after a township revaluation, May 1. The petition has to reach the county before close of business that day, and installments through the first quarter stay payable while the case is open. Evidence is up to five comparable sales, since neighbors' assessments carry no weight. The township's own breakdown puts the average assessment at $227,000, a useful yardstick when you compare your notice to the street around you.

Appeal only the value, never the amount of tax. Your argument is what the house was worth on the October 1 that precedes the tax year, set against the town's average ratio. If the county board lowers the value, that judgment holds for the year and the two that follow unless a revaluation or an added assessment changes it. After the board rules, the Tax Court of New Jersey takes any further case, filed within 45 days.

A sale can go ahead with tax owing, because the balance is cleared out of the seller's money at the table. Request a payoff statement dated for your closing day, and hand the latest bill to the title company so the next installment goes to the right place.

Ten days from each due date, stretched past a weekend or holiday to the next working day. The office has to have the money in hand by then, as postmarks carry no weight.

Pay at the Tax Collector's Office, 820 Mercer Street, Room 108, by mail, online, by phone or through bank bill-pay. Call 856-488-7880 for help.

Yes. A 10 percent cut on the residential sewer fee goes to owner-occupants aged 60 or more who show proof of age.

Eight percent per year covers the first $1,500 late and 18 percent the rest, charged back to the original due date.

The county board in Blackwood, at 509 Lakeland Road. Filing closes April 1, or May 1 when the township has just completed a revaluation.

Where is Lakewood, NJ, and how big has it become?

Lakewood is a township in Ocean County, New Jersey, and the county's most populous municipality. Wikipedia lists 24.68 square miles of land on the flat coastal plain, with the North Branch of the Metedeconk River along its northern edge and four man-made lakes inside the township. Brick Township, Jackson Township and Toms River border it in Ocean County, and Howell Township lies across the line in Monmouth County.

The township was incorporated in 1892 from part of Brick Township, and much of its housing stock arrived after the 1960s, when woods and cranberry bogs gave way to subdivisions. Population then climbed fast: 60,352 in 2000, 92,843 in 2010 and 135,158 in 2020. By the 2025 estimate, 143,765 people live in the township.

For a seller, that growth shows up in the tax records. Parcels range from older single-family lots near the lakes to newer builds and large condominium communities, so two houses a few blocks apart can carry very different assessments.

Who works on Lakewood property tax inside the Municipal Building?

Two desks inside the Municipal Building at 231 Third Street, Lakewood, NJ 08701, split the work. The Tax Assessor fixes the assessed value of each parcel, while the Tax Collector mails the bill and receives payment. The county tax board in Toms River hears assessment appeals.

  • Tax Assessor: 732-364-2500, extension 5248, open 8:30 AM to 5 PM according to the township assessor page. Ownership records, name and address changes and senior, disability and veteran deduction forms go through this office.
  • Tax Collector: 732-364-2500, open 9 AM to 5 PM according to the township collector page. Bring payment questions, payoff requests and tax sale concerns to this desk.
  • Ocean County Board of Taxation: receives appeals at the Courthouse on Washington Street in Toms River.

The collector's page adds that a new deed reaches the tax records when the Ocean County Clerk forwards it to the assessor, and the collector then works from the assessor's file. If a closing is close, ask the assessor to confirm the owner of record so the bill and any payoff request go to the right name.

What are the Lakewood due dates, and what does a late payment cost?

Lakewood taxes are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. The township gives a 10-day grace period, so a payment that reaches the office by the 10th carries no interest. The township counts days from the date it receives payment, and a postmark does not help.

Bills go out once a year in the summer with four coupons. The first two quarters equal half of the prior year's bill, and the last two reflect the rate struck for the current year, so they come out larger if the rate rose and smaller if it fell. The collector also states that an owner stays responsible for the tax even without a bill in hand, and that escrow with a lender does not change that.

Late-payment costs on the collector's page:

  • Interest of 8% a year on the first $1,500 of a delinquency.
  • Interest of 18% a year on every dollar over $1,500.
  • A 6% year-end penalty if the open balance of tax and interest on December 31 exceeds $10,000, with the whole amount then accruing at 18% from January 1.

A balance counts as current once all earlier bills are paid before the next quarter comes due.

What does a Lakewood property tax payoff look like at a sale?

A Lakewood house can be sold with tax owed, because the closing agent pays the open amount out of the seller's proceeds and records the payment. The seller needs a figure from the collector that runs through the closing date, including any accrued interest.

The bigger concern is a tax sale lien. Lakewood must hold a tax sale each year for the previous year's unpaid municipal charges, which covers water, sewer, maintenance liens and taxes. The 2026 online auction notice covered 2025 and earlier delinquencies and listed October 28, 2026 as the sale date. Selling at a tax sale does not transfer the house. A lien goes on the parcel instead, and the buyer of that lien earns interest until it is redeemed.

The collector explains that most lienholders record the lien with the Ocean County Clerk, and clear title cannot be issued while a recorded lien sits on the property. Liens must be redeemed in full with guaranteed funds. A lien held by the township allows foreclosure to begin six months after the sale, and a lien bought by a third party allows it after two years. A seller who sees a certificate on the parcel should ask the collector for the redemption amount before listing or signing a contract.

Owners challenge the assessed value, never the tax itself, and the deadline falls on April 1 of the year at issue. The assessor's page says a filing counts only when it arrives at the Ocean County Board of Taxation, so mail or drop it off with time to spare. The municipality cannot accept a petition meant for the county board.

The assessor mails a postcard notice on or before February 1 showing land, building and total value along with the prior year's tax. The same page lists the practical limits of an appeal:

  • Land and building values cannot be appealed separately.
  • Assessments of neighboring houses are not accepted as evidence of your value.
  • The first quarter's taxes and municipal charges must be paid before the appeal can be completed.
  • Skipping a certificate of occupancy does not avoid an assessment.

The assessor's office will review a value with an owner by appointment before any filing. The state's appeal guide adds that the burden of proof sits with the owner, who should attach three to five comparable sales, and that a county board decision can be taken to the Tax Court within 45 days.

A sale can change eligibility, so a seller who receives a benefit should ask the state program office how a mid-year move affects the claim.

April 1 of the year being appealed, and the petition must be received by the Ocean County Board of Taxation in Toms River. Lakewood's assessor page states that a filing is complete only on receipt, and a petition handed to the township does not count.

The first two quarters are set at half of last year's bill, while the last two reflect the rate struck for the current year. If the budgets of the county, school district and township rose, the second half grows, and if they fell it shrinks.

  • Assessments above $1,000,000 can skip the board and be filed in state Tax Court.
  • Added and omitted assessments are appealed before December 1.
  • A board judgment can be carried to Tax Court inside 45 days.

The board's guidance says not to file until the assessment card has arrived, which is after February 1. After a revaluation, assessments are meant to equal market value as of the prior October 1, so recent Paterson sales before that date are the best evidence. Added or omitted assessment bills are generally sent in October and payable November 1.

Which deductions can lower a Paterson tax bill?

The assessor's page lists three local benefits, each applied for through the assessor with a claim form. The deductions reduce the bill for qualified owners, and the exemption removes it for a narrow group.

Veteran applicants need a copy of the DD-214, and the veteran and senior claim forms can be filed with either the assessor or the collector. How does Paterson's local economy bear on home values?

Paterson's workforce is large and local. The Census shows 63.6% of residents 16 and older in the civilian labor force, with a mean commute of 22.6 minutes, shorter than in Old Bridge or Ocean County. Hospitals and social services took in about $1.37 billion in 2022, and retail sales were about $1.56 billion, or $9,981 per resident, well under the Passaic County figure.

The poverty rate was 21.2% and the share of residents without health insurance under 65 was 21.3%, so many owners have limited room to absorb a surprise tax bill. An owner who misses a first quarter installment should call the collector early, since interest starts on the due date and each skipped quarter adds to the debt.

What happens if Paterson property tax goes unpaid?

Paterson sells unpaid tax liens at an online auction. The city's notice for the sale of 2023 delinquent taxes and municipal charges set the bidding for December 11, 2024 at 10:00 a.m. on the city's New Jersey tax sale site. Parcel lists, delinquency amounts and costs are free to view, and bidding follows the instructions posted on that site.

State law allows an accelerated sale when taxes or liens are still open on the 11th day of the eleventh month of the fiscal year. The city fixes its own late interest inside the state ceiling and may allow ten days of grace. A tax sale certificate is a recorded claim against the parcel, and a seller must redeem or cancel it before title is clear.

  • Request a payoff letter that covers the closing date.
  • Ask the Passaic County Clerk whether any tax sale certificate is on record.
  • Redeem the certificate before closing so title is clear.

What else should a Paterson seller check before listing?

Ask the city for open permits and violations before you list. After Hurricane Irene in August 2011 the Passaic River rose to levels unseen for a century, so buyers may ask about past water in basements. The Paterson School District covers all the area inside the city limits.

Recording happens at the Passaic County Clerk, whose published fee schedule also carries the realty transfer tax table by price band. Because the assessor keeps transfer records, the tax roll changes owners once the deed is recorded.

Where is the Paterson Tax Assessor's Office?

City Hall, 155 Market Street, Paterson. The assessor's page gives weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

When was the Paterson appeal deadline for 2026?

May 1, 2026, because Paterson underwent a revaluation or reassessment that year. The deadline for a regular appeal in other towns is April 1, and that window for 2026 has closed.

How much is the Paterson veteran property tax deduction?

The deduction is $250 a year for a qualified veteran or surviving spouse who owns the home and was a New Jersey resident on the prior October 1. A veteran rated 100% permanently and totally disabled by the VA may qualify for a complete exemption instead.

Does Paterson hold tax sales?

Yes. The city sold 2023 delinquent taxes in an online auction on December 11, 2024. Parcel details are posted on the city's New Jersey tax sale page.

Can I sell a Paterson house that owes property tax?

Yes. The closing agent settles the arrears from the seller's proceeds. First get a payoff letter from the Paterson tax collector, and clear any tax sale certificate before closing.

Old Bridge by the numbers

Who bills and assesses property tax in Old Bridge, NJ?

Old Bridge Township has its own Tax Assessor and its own Tax Collection office, and both sit in the township's government offices. The assessor values each parcel. The collector bills and takes payment at (732) 721-5600, extension 2999. The township belongs to Middlesex County, which means value disputes are heard in New Brunswick.

The township runs an online account system where owners can see current-year and prior-year tax details, confirm that a payment arrived, and pay by bank account or card. The system's help page notes that nominal fees apply to online payments. For the fourth quarter of 2025 the collector kept weekday hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and added a Saturday session on November 8, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. To view a balance online, create a login with the Web Login ID printed on the latest bill. An owner who cannot find the bill can email the collection office to get the ID.

What is Old Bridge Township like?

Old Bridge spreads over 38.18 square miles of land in the Raritan Valley, facing Staten Island across Raritan Bay and roughly 25 miles from New York City. Its 2020 count was 66,876 people; the 2025 estimate of 70,228 is a 5.0% rise. Do not confuse that with the Old Bridge census-designated place, a smaller area of 27,210 people in 2020 inside the township's borders.

The township was Madison Township from 1869 until voters approved the new name in a 1975 referendum, 7,150 to 4,888. It has no single downtown. Instead it is a set of communities: Laurence Harbor, Madison Park, Brownville, Parlin, Cheesequake and the Old Bridge center, with ZIP codes 08857, 08859, 08879 and 07735. Cheesequake Creek, the South River and Matchaponix Brook drain the township.

Survey data for 2020 to 2024 shows 70.4% of homes owner-occupied, a typical home value of $461,000 and a typical household income of $104,587, higher than in Ocean County, Passaic County or Paterson. The mean commute is 36.1 minutes. Routes 9, 18, 34 and 35 cross the township, and the Garden State Parkway crosses the township with Interchange 120 signed for Laurence Harbor and Matawan.

How did Old Bridge grow, and why does it matter for houses?

Old Bridge was mostly farms in its early decades. The population was 1,662 in 1880 and 7,365 in 1950, then tripled to 22,772 by 1960 as farms gave way to subdivisions. The 1980 Census counted 51,406 people, and the extension of Route 18 to the shore brought major change. Lenape people were the first inhabitants, and the Cottrell homestead, built in 1831, still stands at County Route 516 and Cottrell Road.

The growth between 1950 and 1980 shaped most of the township's neighborhoods. Old Bridge's climate is now classed as humid subtropical, so summer humidity and heavy rain are part of the maintenance picture for roofs, siding and crawl spaces. Low ground near Raritan Bay and the creeks needs a closer look at drainage when you prepare a house for showings.

When are Old Bridge property taxes due?

State law sets four installments, mailed ahead of each due date. A grace period of ten days is optional and set by township resolution, and the statutory ceiling on late interest is 8% a year up to $1,500 and 18% above.

A bill that goes out late must give at least 25 days to pay, and interest then runs from the original due date. Old Bridge's fourth quarter bills in 2025 prompted a township statement because the third quarter had been estimated on a 4.79% rise while the final 2025 increase came in near 10%.

Why did Old Bridge tax bills jump in 2025?

The township explained in August 2025 that school tax makes up about 60% of the total property tax bill. The school levy rose 13.87% that year, while the municipal tax rate rose 1.58%. The final 2025 and preliminary 2026 bill went out in late August or early September, and the township pointed owners to the Board of Education at 732-566-1000 for school budget questions.

A third quarter estimate can understate the year, and the fourth quarter then carries the catch-up. Pull the full year's billed and paid amounts from the collector before choosing a closing date, and have the closing agent prorate against the actual bill rather than the estimate.

How do I appeal an Old Bridge assessment?

Owners file with the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, 75 Bayard Street, 4th Floor, New Brunswick, phone 732-745-3350. Petitions can be filed online through an account. Evidence may go up with the petition or as late as seven calendar days before the hearing, by 4:00 p.m., and the system routes the petition to the board, the assessor and the clerk. The board resolved that it will not hold virtual hearings. Its office, which serves twenty-five municipalities, is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m.

  • A regular petition has an April 1 cutoff, moved to May 1 if the township revalued or reassessed.
  • Added and omitted assessment appeals are due December 1, and the county must receive them, not just see a postmark
  • You must be current on taxes through the first quarter of the tax year to proceed.
  • Appeals cover value only, never the tax rate set by the budgets.

Owners unhappy with the board's judgment have 45 days from mailing to go to the state Tax Court, and an assessment over $1,000,000 may start there.

Which relief programs apply to Old Bridge owners?

The state's ANCHOR program gives property tax relief to New Jersey owners and renters who live in the property as a main home and meet income limits. One combined form covers Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ; the 2025 form was due November 2, 2026.

With 17.8% of residents 65 or older in Old Bridge, several programs are worth a look.

  • Senior Freeze reimburses increases in tax on a main home.
  • ANCHOR covers owners and renters under the income limits.
  • Local deductions for veterans, seniors and disabled owners come from the township assessor.

What should an Old Bridge seller check before listing?

The township directory lists a Rent Stabilization Board, a Building and Code department and a Zoning Board, so landlords and anyone with an unfinished project should check each office before a sale. Ask the building department whether permits for a deck, basement or addition are closed, and ask the assessor whether an added assessment is pending.

Deed filing happens at the Middlesex County Clerk, whose office can give the current fee schedule. The collector can issue a payoff letter good through the closing date. All of Old Bridge Township lies within the Old Bridge school district, so school boundaries are the same across the township.

Where is Middletown, NJ, and what shapes its housing?

Middletown is a township in northern Monmouth County and the county's largest municipality by population. Wikipedia gives it 58.72 square miles in total, of which 40.95 are land and 17.78 are water, mostly Sandy Hook Bay, Raritan Bay and the Navesink River. That water frontage explains why a good share of its houses sit near the shoreline or on creek lots.

The township was formed on October 31, 1693 and incorporated under the Township Act of 1798. Railroad service arrived in 1875, and the area slowly turned from fishing and farming villages into a commuter suburb. The township website lists five historic districts: Chapel Hill, Locust, Monmouth Hills, Navesink and Middletown Village.

The township spans eleven ZIP codes, and their postal names include Middletown, Belford, Lincroft, Locust, Navesink, Port Monmouth and Leonardo. A mailing address with one of those names can still sit inside the Township of Middletown for tax purposes, so check the block and lot rather than the postal town.

Which Middletown office does what with property tax?

Middletown splits the job between an assessment office and a collection division, and both sit in the Finance Department at 1 Kings Highway, Middletown, NJ 07748. Assessment questions go to the Tax Assessor, and the collector bills and collects only.

  • Tax Collection: 732-615-2086. Payment hours run 8:00 AM to 3:45 PM and office hours are 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM, Monday to Friday, per the township collection page.
  • Tax Assessor: handles value, ownership and address changes, and senior and veteran relief paperwork. The township's assessment page links to the Monmouth County record search for assessed values, sales and property record cards.
  • Sewerage Authority: 732-495-1010 for delinquent sewer charges, which are billed separately from the tax bill.

The township says the bill combines municipal, library, school, open space and county taxes. Because those levies come from different bodies, the Middletown collector cannot explain a school or county budget line and will direct you to the taxing authority.

What are the Middletown property tax due dates and the grace period?

Middletown taxes are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. A 10-day grace period normally applies, and a tenth day that lands on a weekend or holiday pushes the deadline to the following business day. The last moment to pay without interest is 3:45 PM on the final day of the grace period.

The township states that the State of New Jersey does not accept postmarks, so a payment must be in the office on time. Interest on late payments is governed by N.J.S.A. 54:4-66. Failing to receive a bill does not cancel the tax under N.J.S.A. 54:4-64, so the owner is responsible for asking the collector what is due.

Bills go out once a year. The first-half amount is a preliminary half of the previous year's taxes, and the second-half bill subtracts that estimate from the final total once the rate is set. The collection page asks sellers to hand the bill to the new owner or the buyer's paying agent at closing. A duplicate bill carries a charge.

How does the Middletown tax sale work, and how does it affect a seller?

Every New Jersey municipality must hold at least one tax sale a year, and Middletown runs an accelerated electronic sale. For 2026 the township listed December 17, 2026 as the sale date. Payments received after 3:45 PM on November 10, 2026 had to be guaranteed funds such as an attorney trust check, title company check, cashier's check or money order, and card or ACH payments were unavailable after that time.

An unpaid parcel picks up added costs once it enters the sale process:

  • A 2% cost of sale, with a $15 minimum and a $100 maximum.
  • A $25 mailing fee for each of two scheduled mailings.
  • Delinquent taxes plus interest, added to those fees for the total due.

The township says these fees cannot be waived, and a notice that goes astray does not void the sale. It also warns that a tax lien gives the buyer no right to possess the property, which comes only through foreclosure. A seller who is behind should ask the collector for an exact payoff and give it to the title company early. Cash payments must be exact, because excess cash goes to the next quarter and no change is returned.

How did Middletown's 2026 assessments change, and how are appeals filed?

The township reports that the aggregate preliminary net value of Middletown for tax year 2026 was 7.94% above 2025. Higher total value does not mean every bill rises by that percentage, because the rate falls as total value climbs. An owner whose assessment grew less than 7.94% takes on a smaller share of the municipal levy, and one whose assessment grew more takes on a larger share.

The same page gives the appeal window for 2026 assessments: January 15, or April 1 if the assessment exceeds $1 million. Monmouth County uses an alternate calendar, so the statewide April 1 date does not govern ordinary houses here. Petitions can be filed through secure.njappealonline.com. Changes agreed with the assessor after May 15, 2026 take effect in tax year 2027.

Before filing, compare your value with closed sales on the township's interactive sales map, which leaves out distressed sales. The state's appeal guide says property taxes cannot be appealed, only the assessment, and that evidence should be dated before the October 1 assessment date.

Middletown is a heavily owner-occupied suburb with high incomes and long commutes, according to Census QuickFacts.

Does Middletown's historic designation affect a sale?

It can. The township's Landmarks Commission reviews work on structures inside the five historic districts, and owners planning additions or changes need a Certificate of Appropriateness. A buyer of a house in Middletown Village, Navesink, Locust, Chapel Hill or Monmouth Hills should know that exterior plans may go through that review.

Houses outside those districts follow ordinary township permit rules. If you are unsure which applies, ask the township with the block and lot number from your tax bill.

When is the last day to pay Middletown property tax without interest?

It is the last day of a 10-day grace period after each due date of February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, by 3:45 PM. A weekend or holiday on the tenth pushes the deadline to the following business day.

Yes. Ask the Middletown tax collector for a payoff figure, and your closing agent settles it out of the sale money. If the parcel has entered the tax sale process, added costs apply and guaranteed funds are required.

For 2026 assessments the township lists January 15, or April 1 when the assessment is over $1 million. Monmouth County follows an alternate calendar, and filing can be done through secure.njappealonline.com.

Who do I contact if my Middletown sewer bill is overdue?

Call the Township of Middletown Sewerage Authority at 732-495-1010. Delinquent sewer charges are separate from the property tax bill, and the township said it would sell delinquent sewer charges in 2026.

Does a postmark count for a Middletown tax payment?

No. The township says New Jersey does not accept postmarks, so the payment must be received in the office by 3:45 PM on or before the last day of the grace period.
